name: Dismissal by Reframing
description: Restates an opposing argument as what it is 'really' about, then responds to the restatement.

name: Causal Totalization
description: Names one person, group or entity as the cause of broad or total harm, with no mechanism or bounded scope.

name: Monocausal Blame
description: Reduces a complex outcome to a single cause or actor ('because of X, everything has fallen apart', 'the only reason', 'it's all X's fault').

name: Totalizing Harm Language
description: Uses absolute, sweeping harm language ('destroying everything', 'completely ruined') without a bounded claim, evidence or mechanism.

name: Settled Law Dismissal
description: Answers a legal argument with 'well-settled law' or an equivalent phrase, with no engagement with the argument in the same passage.

name: Merit Dismissed Without Engagement
description: Dismisses a legal argument as frivolous, meritless, or vexatious without substantively addressing the argument itself.

name: Authority Weight Stacking
description: Appeals to the weight or number of authorities ('the weight of authority', 'every court to consider') in place of the reasoning of any one of them.

name: Sanctions Raised
description: Raises sanctions or a disciplinary referral in response to an argument or filing. Sanctions are sometimes warranted; the rule marks the phrasing so a reader can check whether the argument itself is also answered. It names no court, statute or rule number, so the same wording counts in every jurisdiction.

name: Procedural Bar Raised
description: Answers an argument with a procedural bar such as waiver, preservation, standing or timeliness. Procedural bars are often valid; the rule marks the phrasing so a reader can check whether the merits are also addressed.

name: Opposing Position Restated in Absolute Terms
description: Restates the opposing party's argument in absolute terms ('plaintiff argues that all ...', 'is essentially asking this court to ...'), then responds to the restatement.

name: Loaded Descriptor in Reporting
description: Describes a person, group or measure with a loaded adjective ('controversial', 'embattled', 'so-called') in the writer's own voice rather than attributing it to a source.

name: Anonymous or Unverifiable Source Attribution
description: Attributes a claim to unnamed or unverifiable sources ('sources familiar with', 'critics say', 'insiders reveal'). Anonymous sourcing is sometimes necessary; the rule marks it so a reader can weigh it.

name: Vague Quantifiers
description: Uses vague quantifiers ('many believe', 'some experts', 'it is widely thought') that suggest broad agreement without a verifiable claim.

name: Minority and Majority Views Paired
description: Pairs what 'some say' with what 'most experts' say in the same passage, presenting the two as a debate. Whether the balance is fair depends on the evidence, which the rule does not check.

name: Emotional Lead
description: Opens with emotionally charged wording ('shocking', 'bombshell', 'outcry') in its first sentence, before the facts are given.

name: Late Qualifier
description: Places a qualifier, denial or correction ('however, ... no evidence', 'but ... could not be confirmed') late in the text, after at least 200 characters of framing.

name: Scare Quotes
description: Puts a single word or short fragment in quotation marks next to a noun such as 'policy' or 'plan', which can signal doubt or irony without stating an argument.

name: Loaded Attribution Verbs
description: Uses loaded attribution verbs ('claimed', 'insisted', 'admitted', 'lashed out') rather than neutral ones ('said', 'stated'). Two or more are needed to trigger the rule.

name: Speculation Presented as Likely
description: Presents a possible outcome as likely with directional hedges ('is expected to', 'could soon lead to', 'raises the specter of'). Two or more are needed to trigger the rule.

name: Survivorship Framing
description: Draws a conclusion from winners only ('top funds all use', 'every successful investor has', 'a $10,000 investment in ... would now be worth'), with no mention of the ones that failed.

name: Chosen Reference Point
description: Measures a price against a chosen reference point ('down 50% from its all-time high', 'up 200% from the lows'), which shapes how the number reads.

name: Chosen Timeframe
description: Pairs a chosen start date or period ('since March', 'since the bottom', 'in the last five years') with a return or a comparison, so the choice of dates carries the claim. Month names are calendar words, not entities.

name: Projection Stated as Fact
description: States a forecast as a certainty ('the stock will reach', 'revenue will hit', 'guaranteed returns') without a qualifier such as 'is projected to'.

name: Trend Extrapolation
description: Extends a recent track record into the future ('has consistently outperformed', 'continues its streak', 'no reason to think this will stop').
